about: The IA Design Challenge is a team design project in Cambridge's Engineering Tripos Part IA, run in the Lent Term and Easter vacation with Engineers Without Borders UK as part of its annual Engineering for People Design Challenge. A short lecture series introduces a structured design process (investigating the context, defining the problem, generating ideas, selecting and refining solutions, and communicating the design), and teams apply it to a real context described in an EWB-UK briefing pack. It is coursework for standard credit: in 2026-27 a team poster (out of 6) and video (out of 10) give 16 marks, with 12 qualifying. This guide explains the course and the design methods it relies on; it does not invent a syllabus.

notes.h: What the Design Challenge is and how it is assessed
notes.body:
The IA Design Challenge is a team design project in Part IA of the Cambridge Engineering Tripos. It is coursework rather than an examined lecture course, and it has no fixed technical syllabus: what you design depends on the year's brief and on your team's choices.

What the department says it is
- The 2026-27 Part IA guide describes it as an introduction to a structured design process and to the role of design in developing innovative products, systems and services.
- Teams tackle a real-world design challenge, focusing on social, environmental and economic factors.
- It is run with Engineers Without Borders UK (EWB-UK) as part of EWB-UK's annual national Engineering for People Design Challenge. EWB-UK provides a briefing pack describing a specific real-world context in which you identify design problems and opportunities.
- It runs over the Lent Term and the Easter vacation.

Structure (from the 2025-26 syllabus page, the most recent readable; check Moodle for 2026-27)
- Five lectures in Lent (two in each of weeks 1 and 2, one in week 8), with two further slots, in weeks 7 and 8, reserved for group work.
- No prerequisites, but the coursework may draw on IA Exposition, IA Engineer in Society, IA CAD and IA Drawing.
- Aims: show the role of design in engineering, introduce a structured design process, provide a real-world challenge and give an opportunity for teamwork.
- Full coursework requirements are on Moodle.

How it is assessed (2026-27 credit notice)
- Team work, with a poster marked out of 6 and a video marked out of 10.
- Total 16 marks on a 0-16 scale, with a qualifying mark of 12 for satisfactory work.
- Like all Part IA coursework it is for standard credit: marks are capped at the qualifying level, and you need to complete every activity to receive the full qualifying mark. Shortfalls reduce the coursework total that counts towards the Tripos total.

What the course content is
- The 2025-26 syllabus page sets out a four-stage process: investigating the context, defining the problem, generating solution ideas, and selecting and refining solutions. A fifth heading covers communicating about design to the right audiences. The other notes in this guide take these in turn.

Exam tips: there is no exam. Read the EWB briefing pack and the Moodle requirements early, agree team roles and deadlines straight away, and plan backwards from the poster and video submission dates.

notes.h: Investigating the context and defining the problem
notes.body:
The syllabus starts with understanding the context and turning it into a clear problem. Many weak design projects fail here: they jump to a gadget before understanding who it is for and what really matters. The methods below are widely used in engineering design. Use the ones your lectures and Moodle materials recommend.

Investigating the context
- Read the EWB briefing pack carefully. It is your main evidence about the place, the people, their resources and their constraints.
- Identify stakeholders: the people who will use, pay for, build, maintain or be affected by a solution. List what each group needs and what limits them.
- Look across social, environmental and economic factors, which the course explicitly highlights. Ask, for example: Who would own and maintain this? What local materials and skills exist? What happens at the end of its life?
- Look for opportunities, not just problems. Something that already works locally may be worth building on.
- Record where each piece of evidence comes from, so you can justify your choices later and avoid assumptions that do not fit the community.

Defining the problem
- Write a problem statement that says who has the need, what the need is and why it matters, without naming a solution. "Families need a reliable way to store harvested grain without loss to damp and pests" leaves room for many designs; "design a metal silo" does not.
- Turn the statement into requirements. Separate must-have requirements (if a design misses one, it fails) from desirable ones (more is better).
- Make requirements testable where possible, for example a cost limit, a capacity, or something that can be repaired with locally available tools.
- Check the requirements against the context. A requirement that cannot be met with the community's resources needs rethinking.

Scoping
- A good scope is narrow enough to tackle properly within a term but significant enough to matter. Agree the scope as a team and revisit it once you know more.

Exam tips: strong design work shows a clear line from evidence about the context, to the problem statement, to the requirements, to the final design. Keep that line visible in your poster and video.

Once the problem and requirements are agreed, the course moves to generating solution ideas, then selecting and refining them. Good design separates diverging (creating many options) from converging (choosing between them). The methods below are standard engineering design tools.

Generating ideas
- Brainstorming: generate many ideas quickly without judging them, then build on each other's ideas. Quantity first; evaluation later.
- Function breakdown: split the overall function into sub-functions (for example collect, store, protect, dispense) and generate ways to achieve each one.
- Morphological chart: list sub-functions as rows and possible means for each as columns, then combine one means from each row to make complete concepts. This makes it easy to explore combinations you might not have thought of.
- Look at existing solutions, both local and elsewhere, and at analogous problems in other fields.
- Sketch. Quick sketches communicate ideas within a team far better than words, and the IA Drawing skills help here.

Selecting
- Screen out concepts that fail any must-have requirement.
- Pugh's concept selection method compares each concept with a reference (datum) concept, criterion by criterion, scoring better (+), worse (−) or same (S). It helps teams discuss strengths and weaknesses and combine the best features of several concepts.
- A weighted decision matrix scores each concept against weighted criteria. For example, with weights cost 0.40, social impact 0.35 and feasibility 0.25, a concept scoring 3, 5 and 4 (out of 5) totals 0.4 × 3 + 0.35 × 5 + 0.25 × 4 = 3.95, and one scoring 5, 3 and 3 totals 2.00 + 1.05 + 0.75 = 3.80.
- Treat the totals as an aid to discussion, not an answer. Check how sensitive the ranking is to the weights. In the example a small change in weighting could reverse the order, so the reasoning matters more than the number.

Refining
- Develop the chosen concept in more detail: size it, choose materials, and estimate cost and performance using your IA engineering knowledge.
- Test against the requirements and the context. Simple prototypes, models or calculations expose problems early.
- Iterate. Design is rarely linear, and it is normal to return to the problem definition when you learn something new.

Exam tips: show that you considered several genuinely different concepts and explain why you chose one. A single idea taken straight to detail is a common weakness.

notes.h: Communicating the design and working as a team
notes.body:
The final heading on the 2025-26 syllabus page is communicating about design to the right audiences, and its objectives include communicating both how the context relates to your solution and the process you followed, including how you worked as a team. In 2026-27 this is assessed through a team poster (out of 6) and a team video (out of 10).

Communicating the design
- Know your audience. Assessors want to see your reasoning; a community or a client would want to know what the design does for them and what it needs from them. Pitch the language and level of detail accordingly.
- Tell a clear story: context, then problem, requirements, concepts, selection, final design and evaluation. Each step should follow from the one before.
- Show, don't just tell. Use clear sketches, CAD images, diagrams and a small amount of key data. The IA CAD and Drawing courses give you the tools.
- Be honest about limitations and next steps. A credible design acknowledges what has not been tested and what could go wrong.

Posters
- Have one main message that is readable from a distance, a logical reading order, and large visuals with short text.
- Cut anything that does not support your argument.

Videos
- Plan a storyboard and script before filming, agree who presents which part, and keep to time.
- Check the sound quality. Clear audio matters more than fancy editing.
- Rehearse so the explanations are concise. The IA Exposition course's presentation skills apply directly.

Working as a team
- Agree roles, ways of communicating and internal deadlines at the start, and keep a shared record of decisions and evidence.
- Divide the work so that everyone contributes to the design thinking, not only to production of the outputs.
- Deal with disagreements early by going back to the evidence and the requirements. If problems persist, raise them with the course organisers in good time.
- Reflect on the process. The objectives explicitly include communicating your process, so be ready to explain how the team worked and what you would do differently.

Exam tips: plan the poster and video from the start of the project, not the end. Collecting sketches, photos of models and decision records as you go makes the final outputs much easier and better.

questions.q: Criteria weights are cost 0.40, social impact 0.35 and feasibility 0.25. Concept P scores 4, 4, 2 and concept Q scores 2, 5, 5 (out of 5). Which is true?
options: P scores 3.50 and Q scores 3.80, so Q ranks higher
P scores 3.33 and Q scores 4.00, so Q ranks higher
P scores 3.20 and Q scores 4.25, so Q ranks higher
P ranks higher, because it scores better on cost, the most heavily weighted criterion
questions.why: P = 0.40×4 + 0.35×4 + 0.25×2 = 1.60 + 1.40 + 0.50 = 3.50. Q = 0.40×2 + 0.35×5 + 0.25×5 = 0.80 + 1.75 + 1.25 = 3.80, so Q ranks higher. The 3.33 and 4.00 pair are plain averages of the scores (10/3 and 12/3), which ignore the weights. The 3.20 and 4.25 pair come from applying the weights in reverse order (0.25 to cost and 0.40 to feasibility). Saying P wins because it beats Q on the heaviest criterion ignores the other two: Q's lead on social impact and feasibility outweighs P's lead on cost once every weighted score is added.

questions.q: Which is the best problem statement at the start of a design project?
options: Households need a dependable, affordable way to get clean drinking water close to home
Use a morphological chart to choose a pump
questions.why: A good problem statement describes who needs what and why, without fixing a solution. The pump options already name a solution (and one makes cost the only goal), and the last describes a method, not a problem.
